question: Who is the person described?

positions.position: Al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, also called Ubayy, the Thaqafi ally of Banu Zuhra.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL:2:204-206/r1 (MUQATIL; reports): Muqatil: al-Akhnas professed love for Muhammad and swore to follow Islam; the Prophet welcomed him although he intended otherwise. MUQATIL:2:204-206/r9 (MUQATIL; reports): Muqatil: al-Akhnas was called Ubayy ibn Shariq; he turned 300 Banu Zuhra men back from Badr, reasoning Muhammad was their nephew whether truthful or false. TAB-FULL:v3p572/r2 (TAB-FULL; reports): Al-Suddi: al-Akhnas professed Islam and swore sincerity, then burned Muslim crops and killed donkeys, occasioning 2:205. TAB-FULL:v3p572/r3 (TAB-FULL; holds): Al-Tabari: aladd al-khisam is crooked contention; associates Akhnas with 104:1 and 68:10-13. IBNABIHATIM:v2p363/r6 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddī says the verse was revealed about Akhnas ibn Shurayq, an ally of Banū Zuhra. IBNABIHATIM:v2p364/r3 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddī says Akhnas claimed to the Prophet that he sought Islam and was truthful. THALABI:v2p119#2/r1 (الكلبي والسدي ومقاتل وعطاء; reports): Al-Kalbi, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and Ata say the verse concerns al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, a polished hypocrite who professed love for Muhammad, withdrew Banu Zuhra at Badr, then destroyed crops and livestock. MAWARDI-FULL:v1p264/r16 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddi says these verses were revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p65/r3 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddi identifies the hypocritical speaker as al-Akhnas ibn Shariq: after professing sincerity to Muhammad, he burned Muslim crops and hamstrung their donkeys, prompting the next verse. WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p74/r1 (الكلبي والسدي ومقاتل وابن عباس في رواية عطاء; reports): They say the verse was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, called Akhnas because he withdrew with 300 men of Banu Zuhra from Badr; he charmed the Prophet, professed Islam and love, swore sincerity, and was a hypocrite inwardly. WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p74/r2 (author; holds): The qualification in worldly life reflects his lying: the Prophet was not truly impressed with his words, and al-Akhnas earns no afterlife reward for them. WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:203-204/r5 (author; holds): The person is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, a hypocrite with smooth speech and a good public face but evil inward character. WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:203-204/r7 (author; reports): Al-Akhnas used to swear to the Prophet that he believed in him and loved him. JISHUMI:v1p833#2/r10 (السدي والكلبي; reports): Al-Suddi and al-Kalbi say the verse concerns al-Akhnas al-Thaqafi, an ally of Banu Zuhra, whose name was Ubayy; he persuaded them to withdraw from Badr by saying Muhammad was their nephew, then charmed the Prophet with public Islam while concealing hostility. BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p235#2/r1 (الكلبي ومقاتل وعطاء; reports): Al-Kalbi, Muqatil, and Ata say the passage was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, an ally of Banu Zuhra, also named Ubay; he withdrew from Badr with three hundred men, was charming in speech and appearance, feigned Islam and love for the Prophet, and was a hypocrite whom the Prophet drew near. KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p278#2/r2 (author; holds): The man is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, eloquent and smooth-tongued; he softened his speech to the Messenger, professed love and Islam, and claimed God knew he was truthful. IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p278#2/r1 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddi says the passage concerns al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq (whose name he gives as Ubay): he professed Islam, claimed sincerity, then burned Muslim crops and killed their donkeys. IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p281/r9 (author; reports): If the earlier verses concern hypocrites who spoke about al-Rajiʿ, this one concerns its martyrs; if they concern al-Akhnas, this one concerns the first Anṣar and Muhājirūn to believe. TABRISI:2:204-205/r15 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddī identifies the referent as al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who displayed affection for the Prophet and Islam while concealing the opposite. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r1 (ابن عباس والسدي ومقاتل; reports): They say the verse concerns al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, whose gentle speech and professions of love and following Islam concealed unbelief and hostility. RAZI-FULL:v5p167#2/r4 (الرواية الأولى; reports): One report identifies al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, an ally of Banū Zuhra, who professed Islam, claimed love for the Prophet, then burned a Muslim’s crops and killed livestock. RAZI-FULL:v5p167#2/r5 (قال آخرون; reports): Another account says al-Akhnas advised Banū Zuhra to withdraw from Badr, claiming they would benefit whether Muhammad was truthful or false; he withdrew with 300 men. RAZI-FULL:v5p170/r5 (المفسرون; reports): Exegetes say the verse was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, and also connect him with verses in al-Humaza and al-Qalam. | mentions 104:1, 68:10, 68:11 QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r2 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddi and other exegetes say the verse concerns al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who withdrew at Badr with 300 allies, later professed Islam to the Prophet, then burned Muslims' crops and killed their donkeys. QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r3 (المهدوي; reports): Al-Mahdawi says the al-Akhnas account also occasioned 68:10–11 and 104:1. | mentions 68:10, 68:11, 104:1 BAYDAWI-FULL:2:204/r6 (قيل; reports): One reported occasion identifies the man as al-Akhnaṣ ibn Shurayq al-Thaqafī, handsome and eloquent, who professed loyalty to the Messenger and Islam. NASAFI-FULL:v1p99#2/r1 (الأخنس بن شريق; reports): The verse was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq: he spoke sweetly to the Messenger, professed love and Islam, and claimed God knew he was sincere. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p324/r6 (عطاء والكلبي ومقاتل; reports): A reported occasion identifies al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, also called Ubayy, as a smooth-tongued, attractive man who professed love and Islam to the Prophet, concealed his intent, then burned Thaqif's crops and killed their livestock after a dispute. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p324/r7 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddi's version says al-Akhnas passed Muslim crops and donkeys, burned the crops, and spared the donkeys. IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p562#2/r1 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddi says the verse was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who professed Islam to the Prophet while concealing the opposite. DURR-FULL:v1p571/r6 (أبو إسحق; reports): Abu Ishaq names the Quraysh men who joined in killing Khubayb: ʿIkrima ibn Abi Jahl, Saʿid ibn ʿAbd Allah, al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, ʿUbayda ibn Hakim, and Umayya ibn Abi ʿUtba. DURR-FULL:v1p572/r1 (author; reports): The continuing report says the verse concerns al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who professed sincere Islam to the Prophet in Medina, impressed him, then burned a Muslim’s crops and hamstrung his donkeys after leaving. DURR-FULL:v1p572/r2 (الكلبي; reports): Al-Kalbi says the verse refers to al-Akhnas ibn Shariq; a descendant of al-Akhnas asked him not to name anyone until leaving Mecca, claiming the Qur’an was revealed about Meccans. ITQAN:v4p382#2/r2 (author; holds): Concealing an individual's name can protect him and make the description more effective in winning sympathy; the unnamed person here is al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who later became a good Muslim. ITQAN:v4p382#2/r3 (author; holds): The unnamed man described as pleasing in speech in worldly life is al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who later embraced Islam and practiced it well. ITQAN:v4p384/r9 (author; holds): The person whose speech impresses the listener is al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq. SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p40/r2 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddi identifies al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq: he professed Islam to the Prophet, then burned Muslims’ crops and hamstrung their donkeys, prompting the verse. ALUSI-FULL:v2p94#2/r5 (السدي; reports): Al-Suddī says the verse was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq, who professed Islam to the Prophet, then burned Muslim crops and hamstrung their donkeys. ELMALILI:2:203-207/r20 (author; reports): The verses were revealed about Ahnes ibn Sharik of Banu Thaqif, an ally of Banu Zuhra, who professed Islam and love to the Prophet, then burned a Muslim field and killed livestock after leaving. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p263/r6 (author; holds): Al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi outwardly displayed affection and faith; Ibn Ashur says his case will be discussed under 2:204. | mentions 2:204 STUDYQURAN:2:204/r2 (some commentators; reports): Some commentators identify Akhnas ibn Shurayq al-Thaqafī as a hypocrite who feigned interest in Islam and claimed God knew his heart.

positions.position: The hypocrites generally: their outward words conceal unbelief or a contrary inward state.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL:v3p572/r6 (TAB-FULL; reports): Other interpreters: applies generally to all hypocrites with divergent inner and outer states. TAB-FULL:v3p576/r4 (TAB-FULL; reports): Qatada: speaker is a hypocrite. IBNABIHATIM:v2p364/r2 (قتادة; reports): Qatāda identifies the person as a hypocrite. NAHHAS:v1p297/r9 (الحسن; reports): Al-Ḥasan identifies the person whose speech impresses as a liar; other reported identifications are a wrongdoer or a hypocrite. JISHUMI:v1p835/r1 (الحسن; reports): Al-Hasan says the verse concerns hypocrites. TABRISI:2:204-205/r14 (الحسن; reports): Al-Ḥasan says the verses were revealed about the hypocrites generally. TABRISI:2:204-205/r16 (author; holds): The passage turns from the previously described believers and unbelievers to the condition of hypocrites. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r2 (الحسن وقتادة وابن زيد; reports): Al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd take the verse generally as concerning a hypocrite whose outward speech differs from his heart. BAYDAWI-FULL:2:204/r7 (قيل; reports): Another reported view says the verse concerns all hypocrites. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p325/r2 (قتادة وابن زيد; reports): Qatada and Ibn Zayd say the verse addresses every hypocrite whose tongue says what the heart does not contain. IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p562#2/r3 (قتادة، ومجاهد، والربيع ابن أنس وغير واحد; prefers): They take the contrast as general: the hypocrites' traits apply to hypocrites broadly and the self-sacrifice to believers broadly; Ibn Kathir calls this correct. BIQAI-FULL:v1p383#2/r2 (author; holds): The dangerous case is a hypocrite who secretly seeks worldly gain while publicly presenting himself as seeking the afterlife. ELMALILI:2:203-207/r21 (müfessirînin ekser-i muhakkikīni; reports): Most authoritative exegetes say the passage applies generally to all hypocrites who display these traits, not only its specific occasion. ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p81/r1 (ABDURRAZZAQ; reports): Qatada identifies the speaker as a hypocrite. MAWARDI-FULL:v1p264/r15 (ابن عباس، الحسن; reports): Ibn Abbas and Hasan say the person described here and in the following verses is a hypocrite. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:204/r4 (author; reports): Reports connect the revelation to hypocrites who appeared friendly before the Prophet and acted destructively behind his back.

positions.position: Anyone with the described deception, including hypocrites, show-offs and other sinners.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL:v3p572/r6 (TAB-FULL; reports): Other interpreters: applies generally to all hypocrites with divergent inner and outer states. TAB-FULL:v3p576/r2 (TAB-FULL; reports): Muhammad b. Kab: that description in 2:204-205; revelation about one man can apply generally. KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p278#2/r3 (قيل; reports): Alternatively, it applies generally to hypocrites, whose tongues are sweet while their hearts are bitter as colocynth. IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p278#2/r4 (قتادة ومجاهد وجماعة من العلماء; reports): Qatada, Mujahid, and other scholars generalize the passage to anyone concealing unbelief, hypocrisy, lies, or harm while speaking otherwise. RAZI-FULL:v5p167#2/r3 (المفسرون; reports): Exegetes differ: some restrict the passage to particular people, while others take it as general for anyone possessing its described traits. RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r2 (أكثر المحققين من المفسرين; prefers): Al-Rāzī prefers the general reading favored by most careful exegetes: the verse covers everyone characterized by these traits, whether or not revelation began with a particular case. RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r3 (محمد بن كعب القرظي; reports): Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī says that even if the verse was revealed about a named person, it can still apply generally to all with those traits. RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r5 (author; holds): A judgment attached to a relevant description signals that the traits cause condemnation, so everyone possessing them deserves blame. RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r6 (author; holds): The general reading gives greater benefit by warning all morally responsible people away from the condemned path. RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r7 (author; holds): Generality is the safer reading: it includes the reported individual, whereas restricting the verse to him would exclude everyone else. QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r6 (قتادة ومجاهد وجماعة من العلماء; reports): Qatada, Mujahid, and others take the verse generally of anyone concealing unbelief, hypocrisy, lies, or harm while speaking otherwise; the next verse then describes the martyrs of al-Rajiʿ. | mentions 2:207 IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p562#2/r7 (محمد بن كعب; reports): Muhammad ibn Ka'b says a verse may be revealed about one man and thereafter have general application. ITQAN:v1p89#2/r3 (محمد بن كعب القرظي; reports): In a conversation with Said al-Maqburi, Muhammad ibn Kab says a verse may be revealed about one person and then apply generally. ELMALILI:2:203-207/r21 (müfessirînin ekser-i muhakkikīni; reports): Most authoritative exegetes say the passage applies generally to all hypocrites who display these traits, not only its specific occasion. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:204/r5 (Râzî; reports): Razi says the verses censure bad qualities rather than particular people, so anyone bearing those qualities deserves censure. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:204/r6 (author; holds): Even if the verses originally concerned one or several hypocrites in the Prophet’s time, their warning applies to everyone who adopts hypocrisy, ostentation, corruption, or destruction. STUDYQURAN:2:204/r1 (IK, R, Ṭ; reports): Most cited commentators prefer to read 2:204–7 as universal teaching on hypocrisy, despite reports of specific incidents. JISHUMI:v1p835/r2 (قيل; reports): Another view says it concerns people who deceive by their tongues and then commit injustice and corruption when they leave. IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p281/r8 (author; holds): The preceding verses appear to concern unbelievers generally; sinners sharing these traits also incur a portion of the warning. DURR-FULL:v1p572/r4 (محمد بن كعب القرظي; reports): Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says the verse may have been revealed about one man while remaining general in application afterward. ASAD-NOTES:2:204#n187/r1 (Asad; rejects): Asad rejects the suggestion that this describes a particular contemporary of the Prophet, finding no valid reason for that identification.

positions.position: The hypocrites who mocked the martyrs of al-Raji.
positions.reasons: IBNHISHAM:v2p174/r1 (IBNHISHAM; reports): Ibn Abbas: after third-year al-Raji detachment with Murthid and Asim was killed, hypocrites mocked them; verse revealed about their words and dead men's reward. TAB-FULL:v3p572/r4 (TAB-FULL; reports): Ibn Abbas: hypocrites mocked al-Raji martyrs as dying pointlessly; verses contrast hypocrites' corruption with martyrs' reward and self-sacrifice. IBNABIHATIM:v2p363/r1 (ابن عباس; reports): After the Rajiʿ expedition, a hypocrite mocked the dead; God revealed this passage about their words and the good those men received. THALABI:v2p120/r1 (ابن عباس والضحاك; reports): Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak say verses through Allah's compassion to servants concern the Raji expedition: Quraysh lured six Muslims with a false conversion request, ambushed them, killed three, and captured Khubayb and Zayd. THALABI:v2p121/r6 (author; reports): After hypocrites reproached the martyrs, the verse was revealed about al-Zubayr, al-Miqdad, Khubayb, and their believing companions, and against those hypocrites. IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p278#2/r3 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbas says the first passage describes hypocrites who disparaged those killed at al-Rajiʿ, naming ʿAsim ibn Thabit, Khubayb, and Ibn al-Dathinna; the following verse refers to its martyrs. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r8 (ابن عباس; reports): Some hypocrites mocked the slain men for not staying home and for failing to deliver their companion's message. QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r5 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas says the verse concerned hypocrites who disparaged those killed at al-Rajiʿ, including Asim ibn Thabit and Khubayb, mocking them for neither staying home nor fulfilling their companion's mission. | mentions 2:207 ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p325/r3 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas reports that hypocrites mocked the Rajīʿ expedition, asking what the men had lost at home and saying they had not delivered their companion's message. IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p562#2/r2 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas says it concerned hypocrites who disparaged Khubayb and his companions, killed at al-Raji; the verses condemn them and praise Khubayb's companions. DURR-FULL:v1p571/r1 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbas says the verse was revealed after hypocrites mocked the Muslims killed in the expedition that included ʿAsim and Mirthad, saying the men had neither stayed with their families nor delivered the Prophet’s message.

positions.position: A particular unnamed pretender to faith.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ:v1p276/r5 (رجل من ثقيف; reports): A report says a man from Thaqīf impressed the Prophet with his speech while inwardly concealing the opposite of his attractive outward presentation. NAHHAS:v1p297/r9 (الحسن; reports): Al-Ḥasan identifies the person whose speech impresses as a liar; other reported identifications are a wrongdoer or a hypocrite. TABRISI:2:204-205/r12 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbās says the three verses were revealed about a hypocritical pretender who outwardly displays what he inwardly opposes. TABRISI:2:204-205/r13 (الصادق; reports): A report from al-Ṣādiq also identifies the verses' referent as a particular person, without naming him here.

positions.position: A liar, as al-Hasan says.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS:v1p297/r9 (الحسن; reports): Al-Ḥasan identifies the person whose speech impresses as a liar; other reported identifications are a wrongdoer or a hypocrite.

positions.position: A wrongdoer, another identification reported by al-Nahhas.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS:v1p297/r9 (الحسن; reports): Al-Ḥasan identifies the person whose speech impresses as a liar; other reported identifications are a wrongdoer or a hypocrite. NAHHAS:v1p297/r10 (author; reports): One reported analysis takes min here as particularized; other authorities identify the person as a wrongdoer or hypocrite.

turns_on: Whether reported occasions restrict the wording or illustrate a general class.

question: What happened to al-Akhnas in the reports?

positions.position: Al-Razi rejects identifying the censured act with the Badr withdrawal, which would not merit blame; he favors the crop burning account.

question: Did al-Akhnas later become Muslim?

positions.position: It is not established that he ever became Muslim.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p278#2/r2 (author; rejects): The author says it is not established that al-Akhnas ever became Muslim. QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r4 (ابن عطية; rejects): Ibn Atiyya says it has never been established that al-Akhnas became Muslim.

positions.position: He later embraced Islam and practiced it well.
positions.reasons: ITQAN:v4p382#2/r2 (author; holds): Concealing an individual's name can protect him and make the description more effective in winning sympathy; the unnamed person here is al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who later became a good Muslim. question: What happened at al-Raji in the reported occasion?

positions.position: A false request for Muslim teachers led to an ambush, deaths and captives; hypocrites mocked the martyrs, while the next verse praises self-sacrifice.
positions.reasons: IBNHISHAM:v2p174/r1 (IBNHISHAM; reports): Ibn Abbas: after third-year al-Raji detachment with Murthid and Asim was killed, hypocrites mocked them; verse revealed about their words and dead men's reward. TAB-FULL:v3p572/r4 (TAB-FULL; reports): Ibn Abbas: hypocrites mocked al-Raji martyrs as dying pointlessly; verses contrast hypocrites' corruption with martyrs' reward and self-sacrifice. TAB-FULL:v3p572/r5 (TAB-FULL; reports): Second Ibn Abbas al-Raji transmission names Asim and Marthad. JISHUMI:v1p833#2/r12 (ابن عباس والضحاك; reports): Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak connect the verse to the al-Rajiʿ expedition: Quraysh falsely claimed conversion and requested learned Companions, so the Prophet sent a party including Khubayb ibn ʿAdi. IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p278#2/r3 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbas says the first passage describes hypocrites who disparaged those killed at al-Rajiʿ, naming ʿAsim ibn Thabit, Khubayb, and Ibn al-Dathinna; the following verse refers to its martyrs. IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p281/r9 (author; reports): If the earlier verses concern hypocrites who spoke about al-Rajiʿ, this one concerns its martyrs; if they concern al-Akhnas, this one concerns the first Anṣar and Muhājirūn to believe. QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r5 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas says the verse concerned hypocrites who disparaged those killed at al-Rajiʿ, including Asim ibn Thabit and Khubayb, mocking them for neither staying home nor fulfilling their companion's mission. | mentions 2:207 QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r6 (قتادة ومجاهد وجماعة من العلماء; reports): Qatada, Mujahid, and others take the verse generally of anyone concealing unbelief, hypocrisy, lies, or harm while speaking otherwise; the next verse then describes the martyrs of al-Rajiʿ. | mentions 2:207 ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p325/r1 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas reports that Quraysh unbelievers deceitfully claimed conversion and asked for teachers; the Prophet sent Khubayb, Murshid, Asim ibn Thabit, Ibn al-Duthanna, and others in the Rajīʿ expedition, where they were killed. Rajīʿ lies between Mecca and Medina; the account is well known in the canonical collections. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p325/r3 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas reports that hypocrites mocked the Rajīʿ expedition, asking what the men had lost at home and saying they had not delivered their companion's message. IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p562#2/r2 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas says it concerned hypocrites who disparaged Khubayb and his companions, killed at al-Raji; the verses condemn them and praise Khubayb's companions. DURR-FULL:v1p571/r1 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbas says the verse was revealed after hypocrites mocked the Muslims killed in the expedition that included ʿAsim and Mirthad, saying the men had neither stayed with their families nor delivered the Prophet’s message. DURR-FULL:v1p571/r6 (أبو إسحق; reports): Abu Ishaq names the Quraysh men who joined in killing Khubayb: ʿIkrima ibn Abi Jahl, Saʿid ibn ʿAbd Allah, al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, ʿUbayda ibn Hakim, and Umayya ibn Abi ʿUtba. SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p40/r1 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas relates that after a raid party including Asim and Mirthad was killed, two hypocrites disparaged them for dying instead of staying home or delivering the Prophet’s message; the verse followed. STUDYQURAN:2:204/r5 (Th; reports): Another reported occasion is that Makkans feigned interest in Islam, requested learned teachers, then ambushed and killed the Prophet’s delegation near Makkah.

positions.position: In the Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak account, six Muslims were lured; three died, Khubayb and Zayd were captured, and later marvels marked their fate.
positions.reasons: THALABI:v2p120/r1 (ابن عباس والضحاك; reports): Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak say verses through Allah's compassion to servants concern the Raji expedition: Quraysh lured six Muslims with a false conversion request, ambushed them, killed three, and captured Khubayb and Zayd. THALABI:v2p120/r2 (ابن عباس والضحاك; reports): In the Raji account, Aasim fought until captured; bees protected his corpse, then rain and a flood carried it away, fulfilling his vow never to touch or be touched by a polytheist. Umar marveled at God's protection. THALABI:v2p120/r3 (ابن عباس والضحاك; reports): The same account praises Khubayb's conduct in captivity: he borrowed a razor, safely held a child while armed, refused treachery, and was miraculously given fruit in Mecca. THALABI:v2p121/r1 (author; reports): The narrative records Khubayb's poem that he did not care which side he fell on for God's cause, and his prayer that God count and scatter his executioners; the author glosses شلو ممزع as dismembered. THALABI:v2p121/r3 (ابن عباس والضحاك; reports): Zayd, whom Safwan bought to avenge his father, said he would not wish even a thorn to hurt Muhammad in exchange for being safe with his family; Abu Sufyan marveled at the Companions' love for Muhammad. THALABI:v2p121/r6 (author; reports): After hypocrites reproached the martyrs, the verse was revealed about al-Zubayr, al-Miqdad, Khubayb, and their believing companions, and against those hypocrites.

positions.position: In Ibn al-Jawzi's detailed account, Asim led six; four died, two were captured, and further reports follow Khubayb's body and its rescuers.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r10 (author; reports): Before his execution, Khubayb requested two units of prayer, then declined to lengthen them lest onlookers call him afraid and recited a poem accepting death for God. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r4 (author; reports): The Prophet sent Khubayb ibn ʿAdi, Marthad al-Ghanawi, Khalid ibn Bukayr, Abdullah ibn Tariq, and Zayd ibn al-Dathina, with ʿAsim ibn Thabit as their commander. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r6 (author; reports): In the fighting, Marthad, Khalid, and Ibn Tariq were killed; ʿAsim shot seven leaders with his seven arrows before the attackers killed him. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r7 (author; reports): ʿAsim prayed that God protect his body after defending God's religion; the attackers sought his head for Salafa bint Saʿd, whose family he had killed, but wasps kept them away. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r8 (author; reports): The attackers waited for evening, but a cloud brought heavy rain and a flood carried ʿAsim's body away. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r9 (author; reports): Khubayb and Zayd were captured; Banu al-Harith bought Khubayb to kill him because he had killed their fathers. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r1 (ابن عباس; reports): Khubayb was crucified alive and asked God to deliver his greeting to the Messenger; when Abu Suruʿa put a spear before him and told him to fear God, it only increased his defiance. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r2 (ابن عباس; reports): Safwan ibn Umayya bought Zayd to avenge his father; Abu Sufyan asked if Zayd would prefer Muhammad in his place, and Zayd answered that he would not wish Muhammad harmed by even a thorn while Zayd was home. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r3 (ابن عباس; reports): After Zayd was killed, the Prophet asked who would recover Khubayb from his gallows for Paradise; al-Zubayr and al-Miqdad went to retrieve him. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r4 (ابن عباس; reports): They found forty pagan men sleeping drunk around the gallows and Khubayb's body still fresh and flexible after forty days. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r5 (ابن عباس; reports): Al-Zubayr carried Khubayb on his horse; when seventy pursuers caught up, he dropped the body and the earth swallowed it. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r6 (ابن عباس; reports): Al-Zubayr identified himself and al-Miqdad as lions protecting their young and offered combat or safe departure; the pursuers left. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r9 (ابن عباس; reports): The report says this verse and the next three were revealed concerning al-Zubayr, al-Miqdad, Khubayb and the other expedition members, as well as the hypocrites. | mentions 2:205, 2:206, 2:207 IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r3 (author; reports): A third occasion is the Rajiʿ expedition: Quraysh falsely claimed conversion and asked Muhammad to send teachers to instruct them. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p218#3/r5 (author; reports): After the group ate dates, a passing woman saw their pits, alerted her people, and seventy men surrounded them between Mecca and Medina. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r7 (ابن عباس; reports): When the two reached the Prophet, Gabriel was with him and said the angels were boasting of these two companions.

positions.position: Another Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak account says seventy riders killed and crucified the dispatched companions.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r1 (ابن عباس والضحاك; reports): Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk report that Quraysh lured the Prophet into sending learned companions, then seventy riders killed and crucified them at al-Rajīʿ; the next verse recalls such martyrs. | mentions 2:207

turns_on: The transmissions differ in their numbers, names and the fate of the captives and bodies.

question: How is min man constructed?

positions.position: Man is a relative pronoun or an indefinite qualified by its clause; it may be nominative as subject or by min's governing relation.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ:v1p276/r4 (ZAJJAJ; holds): Al-Zajjaj: man is nominative either as initial subject or by governing factor in min. NAHHAS:v1p297/r10 (author; reports): One reported analysis takes min here as particularized; other authorities identify the person as a wrongdoer or hypocrite. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p325/r5 (author; reports): من in من يعجبك may be a relative pronoun or an indefinite noun described by the following clause. SAMIN-DURR:2:204/r1 (author; reports): Man may be a relative pronoun or an indefinite noun qualified by the following clause, as in a parallel earlier in the sūra. BIQAI-FULL:v1p383#2/r4 (author; holds): Min al-nās here means either a person or the person who has the described traits.

positions.position: Singular pronouns follow the wording of man although the intended group may be plural.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r4 (author; holds): The phrase “among people” can refer to one person or many; “God is witness” does not prove a singular referent because grammar may follow wording rather than meaning. BURHAN:v3p382/r1 (author; holds): All eight pronouns in this verse agree with the singular wording of man, although the intended meaning is plural.

turns_on: Whether man is relative or indefinite and how its nominative position is licensed.

question: How do singular pronouns agree with man?

positions.position: Eight pronouns agree with the singular wording of man although the meaning can be plural; literal agreement normally comes first.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r4 (author; holds): The phrase “among people” can refer to one person or many; “God is witness” does not prove a singular referent because grammar may follow wording rather than meaning. BURHAN:v3p382/r1 (author; holds): All eight pronouns in this verse agree with the singular wording of man, although the intended meaning is plural. BURHAN:v3p382/r3 (علم الدين العراقي; reports): At the meeting of literal and semantic agreement, starting with the literal form is usual; al-ʿIrāqī says only one Qur’anic passage begins with semantic agreement. | mentions 5:103

positions.position: Grammarians differ over whether a separator is required when switching from semantic to literal agreement.
positions.reasons: BURHAN:v3p382/r7 (ابن عصفور; reports): Ibn ʿAṣfūr reports that Kufans require a separator between clauses when switching from agreement by meaning to agreement by form, whereas Basrans do not; Abū Ḥayyān says usage occurs only with a separator. BURHAN:v3p382/r9 (ابن عصفور; reports): Ibn ʿAṣfūr’s precise rule permits ‘those who rise today and look after our affairs, our brothers’ but bars the same sequence without today as a separator; he says transmitted usage has the separator.

turns_on: Literal agreement can coexist with a plural intended referent.

question: Why leave the person unnamed?

positions.position: Veiling the offender's identity can preserve sympathy and make admonition effective.
positions.reasons: BURHAN:v1p157/r2 (author; reports): The general, unnamed wording ‘among people is one whose speech pleases you’ exemplifies veiling a person’s identity, which can make admonition more effective in winning his sympathy. BURHAN:v1p157/r8 (author; reports): The section lists this verse among Qur’anic examples that leave the offending person unnamed to preserve the possibility of winning him over. ITQAN:v4p382#2/r2 (author; holds): Concealing an individual's name can protect him and make the description more effective in winning sympathy; the unnamed person here is al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who later became a good Muslim.

question: What method identifies unnamed Qur'anic referents?

positions.position: Identification of an unnamed referent requires transmitted evidence; al-Suyuti compiled source-traced reports with reliability judgments.
positions.reasons: ITQAN:v4p384/r1 (author; holds): The science of Quranic ambiguities depends entirely on transmitted evidence; reason alone cannot identify their referents. ITQAN:v4p384/r2 (author; holds): Al-Suyuti says earlier works named ambiguous referents and disagreements without dependable attribution, so he compiled a source-traced work grading sound and weak reports. ITQAN:v4p384/r3 (author; holds): He arranged the book in Quran order and briefly divides ambiguities into two categories, beginning with specified persons and groups whose names are known.

question: Whom does the second-person address mean?

positions.position: Muhammad, whose ear and heart were impressed by the profession.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL:2:204-206/r1 (MUQATIL; reports): Muqatil: al-Akhnas professed love for Muhammad and swore to follow Islam; the Prophet welcomed him although he intended otherwise. IBNABIHATIM:v2p363/r4 (أبو العالية; reports): Abū al-ʿĀliya describes a man with good speech but bad deeds who speaks well to the Prophet. JISHUMI:v1p835/r4 (author; holds): The speech pleases Muhammad and looms large in his heart; the speaker claims belief and loyalty, and invokes God as witness while inwardly concealing the opposite. TABRISI:2:204-205/r17 (author; holds): The hypocrite's speech pleases Muhammad and makes a strong impression.

positions.position: The Prophet if a named incident is intended, or any believer if the class of hypocrites is intended.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p325/r6 (author; reports): The address in يعجبك is to the Prophet if the verse concerns a named person, or to any believer if its subject is the general class of hypocrites.

turns_on: Whether the occasion is a named encounter or a general warning.

question: What does yuʿjibuka convey?

positions.position: His speech pleases, impresses, inclines or looms large to the listener.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ:v1p276/r5 (رجل من ثقيف; reports): A report says a man from Thaqīf impressed the Prophet with his speech while inwardly concealing the opposite of his attractive outward presentation. NAHHAS:v1p297/r9 (الحسن; reports): Al-Ḥasan identifies the person whose speech impresses as a liar; other reported identifications are a wrongdoer or a hypocrite. THALABI:v2p122/r1 (author; holds): Here يعجبك conveys approval and love for good-sounding speech; for disapproval one says عجبت من كذا. WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p74/r2 (author; holds): The qualification in worldly life reflects his lying: the Prophet was not truly impressed with his words, and al-Akhnas earns no afterlife reward for them. WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:203-204/r6 (author; holds): His speech impresses people only in worldly life and earns no reward in the Hereafter. JISHUMI:v1p835/r4 (author; holds): The speech pleases Muhammad and looms large in his heart; the speaker claims belief and loyalty, and invokes God as witness while inwardly concealing the opposite. BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p235#2/r2 (author; holds): The speech pleases the listener and grows weighty in the heart; Arabic uses «I like this» for approval but «I am amazed at this» for dislike or disapproval. KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p278#2/r1 (author; holds): His speech pleases you and looms large in your heart; something amazing is what seems great to the mind. KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p278#2/r5 (author; reports): Alternatively, it modifies “pleases you”: his eloquence impresses in this life, but not at judgment when he stammers or is not permitted to speak. TABRISI:2:204-205/r17 (author; holds): The hypocrite's speech pleases Muhammad and makes a strong impression. RAZI-FULL:v5p169/r1 (author; holds): يعجبك means his speech pleases you and grows large in your estimation, like something wondrous that looms in the mind. RAZI-FULL:v5p169/r2 (author; holds): One reading takes the phrase as speech that impresses when he seeks worldly interests, like admiring someone’s words on a particular matter. BAYDAWI-FULL:2:204/r1 (author; holds): His speech pleases you and grows impressive in your estimation; wonder is perplexity caused by ignorance of what prompted the surprise. BAYDAWI-FULL:2:204/r3 (author; holds): Alternatively, his eloquence delights listeners in this life but not the next, when astonishment and speechlessness overtake him or he is not permitted to speak. NASAFI-FULL:v1p99#2/r2 (author; holds): His speech pleases and impresses; the root sense is something marvelous that looms large in the mind. NASAFI-FULL:v1p99#2/r3 (author; reports): The phrase may modify ‘his speech’: he seeks worldly advantage through professed love, not the afterlife; or it may modify ‘pleases you’: his eloquence charms in this life but fails him in the next. QASHANI:2:204-205/r2 (author; holds): The person whose speech pleases claims love while being a fierce opponent, since he remains in the lower self and heresy; he speaks only in worldly life, not from the heart in the afterlife. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p325/r7 (author; holds): His speech impresses because it appears to accord with the addressee's faith and goodness. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p326/r2 (الزمخشري; rejects): Al-Zamakhshari allows attachment to يعجبك, so the speech impresses in worldly life but not at resurrection when he is held back or barred from speaking; Abu Hayyan calls this remote. SAMIN-DURR:2:204/r2 (author; holds): Iʿjāb is finding something pleasing, inclining toward it, and esteeming it; the hamza makes the verb transitive. SAMIN-DURR:2:204/r5 (author; reports): Fī al-ḥayāt may modify qawlihi: he impresses the listener with claims about worldly affairs because he seeks worldly advantage through false professions of love. BIQAI-FULL:v1p383#2/r5 (author; holds): Yuʿjibuka means that the person's speech pleases the listener and captures his heart; this echoes the hypocrite's deception at the sūra's beginning. DURR-FULL:v1p572/r1 (author; reports): The continuing report says the verse concerns al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who professed sincere Islam to the Prophet in Medina, impressed him, then burned a Muslim’s crops and hamstrung his donkeys after leaving. ITQAN:v4p384/r9 (author; holds): The person whose speech impresses the listener is al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq. BURSEVI:v1p264#2/r2 (author; holds): To be impressed is to find something pleasing, incline toward it, and esteem it; al-Rāghib describes wonder as perplexity at not knowing a thing's cause. BURSEVI:v1p264#2/r3 (author; reports): One reading links the phrase to the speech: the person pleases you by what he says about worldly life, seeking worldly advantage rather than the Hereafter. TABATABAI:2:204-206/r2 (author; holds): The phrase ‘in worldly life’ grammatically modifies ‘pleases you’: the speech pleases in this life because judgment here rests on appearances. STUDYQURAN:2:204/r3 (author; holds): The verb translated impresses can mean please, evoke wonder, cause marvel, or delight.

positions.position: Wonder arises from something exceptional or a cause unknown to the observer.
positions.reasons: THALABI:v2p122/r2 (المفضل; reports): Al-Mufaddal says wonder originally concerns something without a like. JISHUMI:v1p833#2/r3 (author; holds): Aʿjabahu means to please or impress; wonder concerns what is outside the ordinary. TABRISI:2:204-205/r1 (author; holds): Iʿjāb is pleasure in admiring what one finds pleasing; related forms describe wonder, particularly at exceptional beauty. BAYDAWI-FULL:2:204/r1 (author; holds): His speech pleases you and grows impressive in your estimation; wonder is perplexity caused by ignorance of what prompted the surprise. NASAFI-FULL:v1p99#2/r2 (author; holds): His speech pleases and impresses; the root sense is something marvelous that looms large in the mind. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p315/r6 (المفضل; reports): Al-Mufaddal says the root idea of wonder is encountering something unlike anything else. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p315/r7 (الراغب; reports): Al-Raghib describes wonder as perplexity arising from something whose cause the observer does not know. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p315/r8 (الراغب; reports): Al-Raghib says wonder depends on the observer’s knowledge rather than being an intrinsic property of the thing. SAMIN-DURR:2:204/r3 (الراغب; reports): Al-Rāghib defines wonder as perplexity caused by ignorance of a thing's cause, relational rather than an intrinsic quality; a thing that amazes me appears in a way whose cause I do not know. BIQAI-FULL:v1p383#2/r6 (الحرالي; reports): Al-Harali defines wonder as a thing's standing outside its peers, becoming rare in its kind of workmanship. BIQAI-FULL:v1p383#2/r7 (الأصبهاني; reports): Al-Asbahani describes astonishment as a state covering someone who perceives excellence whose cause is unknown. BIQAI-FULL:v1p383#2/r8 (الراغب; reports): Al-Raghib says astonishment depends on whether the observer knows the cause; the thing appears without a known cause to that observer. BURSEVI:v1p264#2/r2 (author; holds): To be impressed is to find something pleasing, incline toward it, and esteem it; al-Rāghib describes wonder as perplexity at not knowing a thing's cause. ALUSI-FULL:v2p94#2/r2 (author; holds): Taʿajjub literally involves perplexity from not knowing a cause; here it figuratively means that the eloquence and sweetness of his speech impress and magnify him, since its cause is known. STUDYQURAN:2:204/r3 (author; holds): The verb translated impresses can mean please, evoke wonder, cause marvel, or delight. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p315/r9 (الراغب; reports): Al-Raghib says “this amazed me” means it appeared in a way whose cause I did not know.

positions.position: The related expression ʿajibtu min can signal disapproval or reproach.
positions.reasons: THALABI:v2p122/r1 (author; holds): Here يعجبك conveys approval and love for good-sounding speech; for disapproval one says عجبت من كذا. BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p235#2/r2 (author; holds): The speech pleases the listener and grows weighty in the heart; Arabic uses «I like this» for approval but «I am amazed at this» for dislike or disapproval. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p315/r10 (author; holds): The expression “I wondered at this” can signal reproach, as in a line by Ziyad al-Aʿjam. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p316/r13 (زياد الأعجم; reports): Ziyad al-Aʿjam’s poem uses wonder reproachfully: he marvels that a man insulted him and he did not hit him. question: What speech is pleasing?

positions.position: An outward profession of Islam, love, loyalty or faith that contradicts the heart.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL:2:204-206/r1 (MUQATIL; reports): Muqatil: al-Akhnas professed love for Muhammad and swore to follow Islam; the Prophet welcomed him although he intended otherwise. IBNHISHAM:v2p174/r2 (IBNHISHAM; holds): Ibn Ishaq: hypocrite displays Islam with tongue while heart contradicts. TAB-FULL:v3p572/r2 (TAB-FULL; reports): Al-Suddi: al-Akhnas professed Islam and swore sincerity, then burned Muslim crops and killed donkeys, occasioning 2:205. TAB-FULL:v3p576#2/r1 (TAB-FULL; reports): Mujahid: pleasing speech is outward public presentation in worldly life. TAB-FULL:v3p576#2/r3 (TAB-FULL; reports): Al-Rabi: good speech, bad deeds; speaks pleasantly to Messenger then leaves to corrupt. TAB-FULL:v3p576#2/r4 (TAB-FULL; reports): Ata: words differ from heart, which God knows. TAB-FULL:v3p576#2/r5 (TAB-FULL; reports): Majority readers: hypocrite calls God to witness profession matches belief, though he lies. TAB-FULL:v3p576/r1 (TAB-FULL; reports): Said al-Maqburi quotes scripture: honey tongues, bitter hearts, soft manners, worldly gain through religion; God threatens bewildering trial. ZAJJAJ:v1p276/r5 (رجل من ثقيف; reports): A report says a man from Thaqīf impressed the Prophet with his speech while inwardly concealing the opposite of his attractive outward presentation. IBNABIHATIM:v2p363/r2 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbās says the speech is what the person displays of Islam with his tongue. IBNABIHATIM:v2p363/r3 (مجاهد وعطاء; reports): Mujāhid and ʿAṭāʾ gloss this as a person's outward presentation in worldly life. IBNABIHATIM:v2p363/r4 (أبو العالية; reports): Abū al-ʿĀliya describes a man with good speech but bad deeds who speaks well to the Prophet. IBNABIHATIM:v2p363/r5 (رسول الله; reports): The Prophet warns of honeyed tongues, bitter hearts, worldly exploitation of religion, and a trial that confounds the forbearing. | mentions 2:205 IBNABIHATIM:v2p363/r7 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbās says the heart contradicts what the person says with his tongue. THALABI:v2p119#2/r1 (الكلبي والسدي ومقاتل وعطاء; reports): Al-Kalbi, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and Ata say the verse concerns al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, a polished hypocrite who professed love for Muhammad, withdrew Banu Zuhra at Badr, then destroyed crops and livestock. question: What guidance does the verse give about trusting appearances?

positions.position: Examine conduct and evidence before trusting professions, especially in judgment or responsibility.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL:2:204#2/r4 (author; holds): The verse advises caution in religious and worldly affairs and scrutiny of witnesses and judges; rulers should investigate rather than rely solely on professions of faith and apparent virtue. ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p327/r9 (author; holds): The verse counsels care in religious and worldly matters and cautions judges not to rely on outward faith or righteousness without examining people's inner states. ELMALILI:2:203-207/r22 (author; holds): The passage teaches that people considered for positions of responsibility should be assessed by their conduct, not merely their words. IBNASHUR-FULL:v2p273/r6 (author; holds): The passage teaches believers to discern inner realities and not be deceived by appearances before testing: a person may speak sweetly and look good while concealing evil and plotting harm. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:204/r11 (author; holds): Although Muslims should generally think well of people, this passage warns that good opinion does not mean credulously trusting every claim or smiling face. | mentions 49:12 RAZI-FULL:v5p167#2/r2 (author; holds): The descriptions encourage sound conduct in hearts and limbs and remind people that God cannot be kept unaware of their inner affairs.

positions.position: Judge people by outward conduct until contrary evidence appears; hidden states belong to God.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI:v1p835/r20 (author; holds): A person may be judged Muslim outwardly even while privately concealing the opposite. QURTUBI-FULL:2:204#2/r7 (author; prefers): Al-Qurtubi holds that people are judged by outward appearances until contrary evidence appears, citing Umar: revelation has ended, good apparent conduct merits trust, and hidden states are God's concern. IBNMAJAH:3930/r1 (النبي; reports): Imran b. Husayn recounts the Prophet rebuking a fighter who killed a man after he professed Islam: no one can inspect his heart; the man's body repeatedly rose from its grave.

positions.position: The Prophet and imams cannot see unseen inward states.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI:v1p835/r21 (author; holds): The Prophet does not know the unseen, and an Imam is even less entitled to that claim; this refutes the Imamiyya. TABATABAI:2:204-206/r3 (author; holds): People cannot see inner realities directly while living in this world; they can infer something of them only from their effects.

positions.position: Early statements protected people on profession alone; Ibn al-Arabi says later corruption called for investigation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL:2:204#2/r5 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم; reports): The objection cites the Prophet's statement that he was commanded to fight people until they profess God's oneness, and his instruction to judge according to what he hears. QURTUBI-FULL:2:204#2/r6 (ابن العربي; reports): Ibn al-Arabi answers that those statements belonged to early Islam, when professing Islam guaranteed safety, whereas corruption later became widespread.

turns_on: How to combine judging outward profession with testing evidence of concealed corruption.

question: How does this passage connect to its neighbors and the sura?

positions.position: It follows the contrast in 2:200–201 between worldly-only seekers and seekers of good in both lives, adding hypocrites and sincere believers.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL:v5p167#2/r1 (author; holds): After describing the unbeliever who asks only for worldly good and the Muslim who asks for good here and hereafter, the passage introduces the hypocrite’s traits. | mentions 2:200, 2:201 QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r1 (author; holds): After contrasting those who ask only for worldly good in 2:200 with believers asking for both abodes in 2:201, the passage turns to hypocrites who profess faith but conceal unbelief. | mentions 2:200, 2:201 ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p325/r4 (author; holds): Following the two kinds of supplicants in 2:200–201, the passage contrasts a sweet-speaking worldly seeker with one who seeks God's pleasure and gives himself for it; the first comes first as in the earlier division. Outer speech should match inner belief. | mentions 2:200, 2:201 BIQAI-FULL:v1p383#2/r1 (author; holds): After discussing those seeking worldly benefit alone and those seeking both worlds, the passage notes the absent type rejecting both and the type seeking only the afterlife. ALUSI-FULL:v2p94#2/r1 (author; holds): This continues 2:200’s division of pilgrims by their remembrance and supplication, adding hypocrites and sincere believers after the disbeliever and believer categories. | mentions 2:200 TABATABAI:2:204-206/r1 (author; holds): These verses classify people by hypocrisy versus sincerity in faith, whereas the preceding verses classify them by whether they seek this world or the next; the connection to the Hajj verses is clear. | mentions 2:200 ASAD-NOTES:2:204#n187/r2 (Asad; holds): He takes the passage generally, following the most reliable authorities, as contrasting people focused only on worldly life with those mindful of the hereafter too. | mentions 2:200, 2:201 ASAD-NOTES:2:204#n187/r3 (Asad; holds): The context makes this a further elaboration of the contrast between two attitudes introduced in 2:200–201. | mentions 2:200, 2:201 KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:204/r1 (author; holds): These verses revisit the earlier contrast between people seeking only worldly benefit and those seeking good in both this world and the afterlife. | mentions 2:200, 2:201 JISHUMI:v1p835/r3 (author; holds): After describing believers and unbelievers, the passage turns to hypocrites.

positions.reasons: TAB-FULL:v3p572/r4 (TAB-FULL; reports): Ibn Abbas: hypocrites mocked al-Raji martyrs as dying pointlessly; verses contrast hypocrites' corruption with martyrs' reward and self-sacrifice. TAB-FULL:v3p588/r4 (TAB-FULL; reports): Ali: the contrasting figures of 2:204-207 fought, by Lord of Kaba. IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p278#2/r3 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbas says the first passage describes hypocrites who disparaged those killed at al-Rajiʿ, naming ʿAsim ibn Thabit, Khubayb, and Ibn al-Dathinna; the following verse refers to its martyrs. IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p220/r9 (ابن عباس; reports): The report says this verse and the next three were revealed concerning al-Zubayr, al-Miqdad, Khubayb and the other expedition members, as well as the hypocrites. | mentions 2:205, 2:206, 2:207 RAZI-FULL:v5p168/r1 (ابن عباس والضحاك; reports): Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk report that Quraysh lured the Prophet into sending learned companions, then seventy riders killed and crucified them at al-Rajīʿ; the next verse recalls such martyrs. | mentions 2:207 QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r5 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn Abbas says the verse concerned hypocrites who disparaged those killed at al-Rajiʿ, including Asim ibn Thabit and Khubayb, mocking them for neither staying home nor fulfilling their companion's mission. | mentions 2:207 QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r6 (قتادة ومجاهد وجماعة من العلماء; reports): Qatada, Mujahid, and others take the verse generally of anyone concealing unbelief, hypocrisy, lies, or harm while speaking otherwise; the next verse then describes the martyrs of al-Rajiʿ. | mentions 2:207 IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p562#2/r3 (قتادة، ومجاهد، والربيع ابن أنس وغير واحد; prefers): They take the contrast as general: the hypocrites' traits apply to hypocrites broadly and the self-sacrifice to believers broadly; Ibn Kathir calls this correct.

positions.position: Reports also associate al-Akhnas with the slanderer of 68:10–13 and the backbiter of 104:1.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL:v3p572/r3 (TAB-FULL; holds): Al-Tabari: aladd al-khisam is crooked contention; associates Akhnas with 104:1 and 68:10-13. RAZI-FULL:v5p170/r5 (المفسرون; reports): Exegetes say the verse was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, and also connect him with verses in al-Humaza and al-Qalam. | mentions 104:1, 68:10, 68:11 QURTUBI-FULL:2:204/r3 (المهدوي; reports): Al-Mahdawi says the al-Akhnas account also occasioned 68:10–11 and 104:1. | mentions 68:10, 68:11, 104:1 ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p324/r8 (author; reports): It is also said that this verse refers to the people described as a slanderous swearer in 68:10 and a backbiter in 104:1. | mentions 68:10, 104:1

question: What does the verse show about Qur'anic expression?

positions.position: Poetry may exceed prose in human eloquence, but an acclaimed poem still reveals flaws when measured against the Qur'an.
positions.reasons: BAQILLANI:v1p155/r1 (أفضل من رأيت من أهل العلم بالأدب; reports): An eminent specialist says prose can accommodate greater eloquence than poetry because poetic form constrains speech and its development. BAQILLANI:v1p155/r2 (من يتقدم في صنعة الكلام; reports): A skilled interlocutor counters that poetry may be more eloquent when it meets the conditions of eloquence and includes the causes of rhetorical beauty. BAQILLANI:v1p155/r3 (author; prefers): The author sides with the poetry view: most Arab verbal brilliance is in poetry, while prose lacks comparable examples, despite the later refinement of letters. BAQILLANI:v1p155/r4 (author; holds): Although poetry narrows expression, it gathers and joins its parts; when fully polished in its genre, no human speech can rival it. BAQILLANI:v1p155/r5 (المتنبي; reports): A report says al-Mutanabbi’s companion questioned his Qur’an reading; his reply that the eloquent Meccan was silenced would, if authentic, show his belief in poetry’s greater eloquence. BAQILLANI:v1p155/r6 (author; holds): To show the Qur’an’s superiority, he proposes examining an acclaimed, well-made poem for flaws, uneven structure, digressions, forced phrasing, and shifts between elevated and low diction.

positions.position: Arabic offers exceptional lexical and rhetorical scope, contributing to the Qur'an's unique inimitability.
positions.reasons: BAQILLANI:v1p31/r1 (author; holds): The Torah, Gospel, and other scriptures are not inimitable in composition, though they may share the Qur’an’s inimitability in reporting unseen matters. BAQILLANI:v1p31/r2 (author; holds): He argues other languages permit less eloquent differentiation: they have fewer names for one thing, less polysemy, and less scope for metaphor, allusion, and varied usage. BAQILLANI:v1p31/r3 (author; holds): The Qur’an’s repeated description as clear Arabic, and its being kept from a foreign tongue, support the special eloquence of Arabic; intelligibility to its first hearers may also be a benefit. | mentions 26:195 BAQILLANI:v1p31/r4 (author; holds): Muslims skilled in both Arabic and other languages recognize that the latter lack Arabic’s degrees of eloquence and stylistic distinction. BAQILLANI:v1p31/r5 (author; holds): The Qur’an’s unique inimitability is confirmed by the fact that neither scriptural communities nor Muslims claimed it for the Torah or Gospel.

positions.position: Poetic simile and imaginative recasting express meaning with subtle force.
positions.reasons: JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p245/r1 (author; holds): Unlike a poet who denies that a patron has fever, al-Mutanabbī imagines the fever daring to attack such a noble man and supplies an imagined excuse for its assault. JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p245/r2 (author; holds): Ibn al-Muʿtazz's speaker denies that his gray hair is age, calling it battle dust; Jurjānī praises this concise denial as a direct way to escape reproach, rather than conceding and defending the grayness. JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p245/r3 (الطائي الكبير; reports): The poet recasts gray hair as the smile of reason and refinement, making a bodily sign of age into intellectual radiance. JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p245/r4 (author; holds): Simile can achieve a magical subtlety that plain description cannot reach, giving poetry unusual power to delight, console, and display eloquence.

positions.position: Announcing a subject by pronoun before explaining it adds emphasis, especially for surprising or contested claims.
positions.reasons: JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p113/r1 (author; holds): Announcing a subject through a pronoun and then explaining it is more emphatic than stating the proposition abruptly, because the advance notice acts like a repeated assertion. | mentions 22:46, 23:117 JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p113/r2 (author; holds): This emphatic construction suits denials, suspicion, false claims, and surprising contradictions, as shown by Qur'anic examples where the added clause confirms or exposes what was disputed. | mentions 3:78, 5:61, 25:3

turns_on: The cited discussions concern poetry, prose, simile, emphasis and the Qur'an's Arabic eloquence.

question: What background rules of Qur'anic readings are cited?

positions.position: The seven ahruf were a permission easing recitation; scholars differ over their identity, exact number and whether they remained after the final recension.
positions.reasons: BURHAN:v1p212/r1 (ابن العربي; reports): Ibn al-ʿArabī says no text or report specifies what the seven are, and scholars have differed over their identification. BURHAN:v1p212/r2 (أبو حاتم بن حبان; reports): Abū Ḥātim ibn Ḥibbān counted thirty-five opinions; one group sees the seven as facilitation for reciters rather than a limiting number, while most hold that they are exactly seven. BURHAN:v1p212/r3 (أبو حاتم بن حبان; reports): Those who limit the seven disagree whether they remain available to read now or applied only at the beginning. BURHAN:v1p212/r4 (القرطبي; reports): Al-Qurṭubī says most proponents of the view that the initial permission later settled on today’s reading include Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna, Ibn Wahb, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Ṭaḥāwī. BURHAN:v1p212/r5 (أكثر العلماء; reports): Among those who hold that the permission settled into one reading, most say this happened during the Prophet’s lifetime; al-Bāqillānī, Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, and Ibn al-ʿArabī chose that view. BURHAN:v1p212/r6 (القاضي أبو بكر بن الطيب وابن عبد البر وابن العربي; reports): The initial allowance eased differences among Arab dialects; as speakers trained and one form sufficed, God abrogated the permission after Gabriel reviewed the Qur’an twice with the Prophet in the final year. BURHAN:v1p226/r1 (بعض المتأخرين; reports): Some later scholars take the seven aḥruf to mean dialects, allowing Arab groups to use their customary pronunciations, such as assimilation, imāla, emphatic articulation, hamza, softening, and lengthening. BURHAN:v1p226/r3 (بعض المتأخرين; reports): On this view the seven aḥruf are the seven canonical readings, all soundly transmitted from the Prophet and compiled in ʿUthmān’s codex; the seven reciters chose among the readings they knew, and each had more than one valid choice. BURHAN:v1p226/r4 (author; reports): The source says Muslims in these generations agree to rely on what is soundly transmitted from the seven; the original allowance was mercy for people who would struggle to abandon their dialects. BURHAN:v1p226/r5 (أبي بن كعب; reports): A report from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb recounts Gabriel telling the Prophet, who was sent to an unlettered community including elderly people, children, and those who had never read a book, that the Qur’an was revealed on seven aḥruf; al-Tirmidhī grades it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

positions.position: Authentic variant readings are all true, Prophetically transmitted, mutually confirming, and associated with reciters through teaching rather than invention.
positions.reasons: NASHR:v1p51#2/r1 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم; reports): In reports about two differing reciters, the Prophet praises each with formulas such as “well done,” “correct,” and “thus it was revealed,” affirming both readings. NASHR:v1p51#2/r2 (author; holds): Unlike juristic disagreement, where one position is true in itself and another may err, every variant reading is true, correct, and from God. NASHR:v1p51#2/r3 (author; holds): Attributing a reading to a Companion means that person was especially precise, frequent, or committed in reciting and teaching it, not that they originated it. NASHR:v1p51#2/r4 (author; holds): Attribution to a reading imam or transmitter denotes selecting, favoring, and consistently teaching a linguistic form until it became associated with that reader; it does not denote invention or personal derivation. NASHR:v1p51#2/r5 (author; holds): The variations also ease recitation and lessen the burden on the community. NASHR:v1p51#2/r6 (author; holds): Their variation reaches the highest eloquence and brevity: each reading can function like a verse, avoiding the length that separate verses for every wording would require. NASHR:v1p51#2/r7 (author; holds): Despite their variety, the readings do not contradict one another; they confirm and explain one another, proving the truth of the Prophet who brought them.

turns_on: The notes discuss seven ahruf, their later status, and the validity of transmitted variant readings.

question: What reports and principles concern the Qur'an's compilation or completion?

positions.position: Companions memorized and compiled the Qur'an; reports name several collectors and offer explanations for the short lists.
positions.reasons: BURHAN:v1p241/r1 (author; holds): Many Companions memorized the Qur’an during the Prophet’s life, and every portion was memorized by numerous people, at least enough for mass transmission. BURHAN:v1p241/r2 (ابن عباس; reports): Ibn ʿAbbās reports that when revelation came, the Prophet summoned scribes and directed where to place the verses; al-Tirmidhī calls the report ḥasan and al-Ḥākim ṣaḥīḥ by the two Shaykhs’ criteria. BURHAN:v1p241/r3 (أنس بن مالك; reports): In al-Bukhārī’s report from Anas, the four who compiled the Qur’an in the Prophet’s time were Ubayy, Muʿādh, Zayd ibn Thābit, and Abū Zayd; al-Bayhaqī prefers this report and Ibn Sīrīn names the same four without dispute. BURHAN:v1p241/r4 (ابن سيرين; reports): Ibn Sīrīn’s report differs over two additional names, variously giving Abū al-Dardāʾ and ʿUthmān or ʿUthmān and Tamīm al-Dārī. BURHAN:v1p241/r5 (الشعبي; reports): Al-Shaʿbī gives another list of compilers, saying Mujammaʿ ibn Jāriya had obtained all but two or three sūras; he adds that among the Prophet’s Companions only ʿUthmān among the caliphs compiled it. BURHAN:v1p241/r6 (أبو شامة; reports): Abū Shāma says al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr argued that far more people had collected the Qur’an in the Prophet’s lifetime; the large number of readers killed at Yamāma and Biʾr Maʿūna supports this. BURHAN:v1p241/r7 (القاضي أبو بكر; reports): One reconciliation is that the named few alone collected the Qur’an in all its revealed modes, aḥruf, and readings. BURHAN:v1p241/r8 (القاضي أبو بكر; reports): A second reconciliation is that only those Companions collected both material later abrogated and erased from writing and material whose written form and recitation remained obligatory. BURHAN:v1p241/r9 (القاضي أبو بكر; reports): A third reconciliation is that only those Companions received the entire Qur’an directly from the Prophet, collecting it from his recitation.

positions.position: A completion prayer is reported from the Prophet, but Ibn al-Jazari grades its chain broken; another completion report is weak.
positions.reasons: NASHR:v2p464/r1 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم; reports): A report attributed to the Prophet gives a prayer at completion of the Qurʾan asking for mercy, guidance, remembrance, knowledge, nightly and daytime recitation, and the Qurʾan as proof. NASHR:v2p464/r2 (author; reports): Ibn al-Jazarī grades the completion prayer report muʿḍal because its narrator Dāwūd ibn Qays was from the tābiʿ al-tābiʿīn; he says he knows no other Prophetic report on completing the Qurʾan. NASHR:v2p464/r3 (أبو هريرة; reports): Ibn al-Jawzī reports from Abū Hurayra that the Prophet prayed standing when finishing the Qurʾan; Ibn al-Jazarī grades it weak because its chain includes al-Ḥārith ibn Shurayḥ, criticized by hadith critics.

turns_on: The named collectors and the grading of completion prayers vary in the reports.

question: What broader topics does Ibn Ashur use this verse's context to explain?

positions.position: Geminated and hamzated verb forms can express abundance or intensification; a proposed physical-versus-abstract distinction is disputed.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r1 (author; holds): When a geminated verb is intransitive, its form usually signals abundance or intensification; the Shafiya states this rule, though abundance can be figurative. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r10 (author; rejects): Ibn Ashur rejects that distinction as rhetorical nicety rather than sound rule: the forms signal real or figurative abundance, not abstract meanings versus physical objects. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r12 (لبيد; reports): Labid’s line pairs the verb قدم with its noun إقدام, illustrating alternation between related verb forms. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r13 (سيبويه; reports): Sibawayh says فعل and أفعل alternate; the proposed distinction concerns the verb’s meaning, not whether its object is a body. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r2 (author; holds): Figurative intensification can treat intellectual labor—finding subtle meanings and choosing exact expression—as extensive work. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r3 (صحار العبدي; reports): Asked by Muawiya about eloquence, Ṣaḥār al-ʿAbdī said to speak without error and answer without delay, then jokingly asked to retract the demand to do both. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r4 (author; holds): The intensive sense of verbal explanation is supported by the Quran’s phrase أحسن تفسيرا in 25:33. | mentions 25:33 IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r5 (author; reports): Whether gemination intensifies a transitive verb is disputed; Ibn Ashur says a speaker may choose it over hamza to imply abundance by association with its intransitive use. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r8 (بعض مشايخ القرافي; reports): A teacher cited by al-Qarafi distinguishes light فرق for meanings and doubled فرّق for bodies, reasoning that more letters convey greater or stronger meaning. positions.position: Tafsir examines Qur'anic wording for meaning and inference, differing from qira'at in its aspect of study.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r14 (author; holds): In technical usage, tafsir is the discipline that explains Quranic words and meanings derived from them, briefly or at length. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r15 (author; holds): The relation between lexical and technical senses of tafsir needs little explanation. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r16 (author; holds): Tafsir’s subject is Quranic wording as examined for meaning and inference. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r17 (author; holds): Tafsir differs from qira’at because disciplines are distinguished by their subjects and the aspects from which they examine them. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r18 (author; holds): Calling tafsir a science is loose: knowledge may mean cognition, the rational faculty, certain belief, or demonstrable universal propositions, none of which describes tafsir’s material. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p10#2/r19 (author; holds): Tafsir usually treats particular concepts, not provable universal propositions: explaining words is verbal definition, while derivation proceeds by entailment.

positions.position: The sura's larger argument moves through intercommunal opposition, Abrahamic worship, qibla, creation and judgment.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p204/r2 (author; holds): The discussion turns to the sanctuary, Abraham and his prayer for descendants, Islam as Abrahamic monotheism, the Kaaba's qibla and Meccan rites; Judaism and Christianity are not Abraham's religion. IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p204/r3 (author; holds): The change of qibla rebuts the People of the Book; purifying souls matters more than facing east or west, and replacing earlier laws with what benefits later peoples is no novelty. | mentions 2:177 IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p204/r4 (author; holds): The argument returns to creation, the disavowal of leaders on Judgment Day, and food prohibitions, ending with people who do not profess Islam but display affection toward Muslims. | mentions 2:164, 2:172 IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p204/r1 (author; holds): The discourse groups Jews, Christians, and polytheists in resentment of Muslims, then distinguishes Jewish-Christian disputes; polytheists are worst for obstructing worship at the sanctuary and sharing hostility to Islam. | mentions 2:105, 2:112, 2:113

question: What related Arabic verbs for action and speech are distinguished?

positions.position: Fiʿl is broad, ʿamal narrower; jaʿala can signal beginning an action such as speaking.
positions.reasons: BURHAN:v4p128/r3 (author; holds): Fiʿl is the broadest among related verbs, applying to speech, thought, and other acts; ʿamal is narrower and covers intention, resolve, and speech. BURHAN:v4p128/r7 (author; holds): Jaʿala may mean beginning or embarking, like kāda and ṭafiqa, with a sense of entering into the action: jaʿala yaqūlu means he began to speak.
